curriculum.title: Python Taster: Build a Game in 20 Minutes
curriculum.description: Free taster. Make Python talk, ask questions, make decisions and repeat, then put it all together into a real number-guessing game.

avatar.handoff_to_practice: Your turn. Fill in the TODO lines.

lessons.title: Make Python Talk
lessons.goal: to print text and let Python do maths.

avatar.text: In 20 minutes you'll build a real game in Python, the language used at Google, NASA and Netflix. Let's start by making the computer talk with print!

code_example.code:
print("Hi! I'm Python.")
print("Seconds in a day:", 60 * 60 * 24)
code_example.description: Watch Python talk, then do maths.
code_example.explanation: Line 1 prints text. Text goes inside quote marks. Line 2 prints some text, then a sum. The star means times. Python works out the answer for you.

avatar.text: Quote marks mean: show these words exactly. No quote marks means: work this out. That's why line 2 shows 86400, not the sum.

question.question: What does print("5 + 5") show?
question.explanation: Yes! Inside quote marks, it's just text.

avatar.on_correct: Yes! Inside quote marks, it's just text.
avatar.on_wrong: Not quite. Quote marks mean show the words exactly, so it shows 5 + 5.

question.question: In Python, the star * means times.

avatar.on_wrong: Not quite. The star is how Python writes times.

question.question: Your turn: on line 3, print Seconds in a year: and the sum 60 * 60 * 24 * 365. Tap Run to test it, then Submit.
question.explanation: Remember: line 2 prints text, a comma, then a sum.

avatar.on_correct: Brilliant! Over 31 million seconds, worked out in a blink.

points: print shows things on the screen.
Quote marks mean: show these words exactly.
Without quote marks, Python works out the answer.

avatar.text: Great start! Here's what you learned.
Next up: Python asks YOU a question.

lessons.title: Python Asks You
lessons.goal: to ask a question and use the answer.

avatar.text: Programs get exciting when they listen to you. Let's make Python ask a question with input!

code_example.code:
name = input("What's your name? ")
print(f"Nice to meet you, {name}!")
code_example.description: Watch Python ask a question and remember the answer.
code_example.explanation: Line 1 asks a question and waits. Whatever you type is saved in a box called name. That box is a variable.

avatar.text: Line 2 has an f before the quote marks. That lets you drop a variable into the text with curly brackets. So {name} becomes whatever you typed.

question.question: In line 1, where is your answer saved?
question.explanation: Yes! The answer goes into the box on the left of the equals sign.

avatar.on_correct: Yes! The answer goes into the box on the left of the equals sign.
avatar.on_wrong: Not quite. The answer is saved in name, on the left of the equals sign.

retry.hint: Look left of the equals sign.

question.question: The f before the quote marks lets you put {name} inside the text.
question.explanation: Correct! f-strings fill in the curly brackets.

avatar.on_correct: Correct! f-strings fill in the curly brackets.
avatar.on_wrong: Not quite. Without the f, it would print {name} exactly.

avatar.text: Nice! Here's what you learned.
Next up: Python makes a decision.

lessons.title: Python Decides
lessons.goal: to make a choice with if and else.

avatar.text: Every game needs decisions. Did you win or lose? Let's teach Python to decide with if and else!

code_example.explanation: Line 1 hides the number 7. Line 2 asks for a guess. int turns your answer into a number. Line 3 asks: is the guess the same as the secret?

avatar.text: Two equals signs mean: are these the same? If yes, line 4 runs. If not, the else part runs. The spaces at the start show which lines belong to each part.

question.question: What does == mean?
question.explanation: Yes! Two equals signs compare. One equals sign saves.

avatar.on_correct: Yes! Two equals signs compare. One equals sign saves.
avatar.on_wrong: Not quite. == asks if two things are the same.

question.question: The else part runs when the guess is wrong.

avatar.on_wrong: Not quite. else runs when the if question is no.

avatar.text: Well done! Here's what you learned.
Next up: making Python repeat things.

lessons.title: Python Repeats
lessons.goal: to repeat code with a for loop.

avatar.text: Computers never get bored. Let's make Python repeat something, with a for loop of just two lines!

code_example.description: Watch one line run three times.
code_example.explanation: Line 1 is a loop. range(3) means: do this 3 times. Line 2 has spaces at the start, so it is inside the loop and repeats.

avatar.text: Line 3 has no spaces at the start, so it is outside the loop. It runs once, after the loop is finished. Change 3 to 1000 and Python happily does it 1000 times.

question.question: How many times does a loop with range(5) repeat?
Done! printed 3 times, because it is in the loop.
question.explanation: Correct, that's false. It has no spaces, so it ran once.

avatar.on_correct: Correct, that's false. It has no spaces, so it ran once.
avatar.on_wrong: Not quite. Line 3 has no spaces, so it is outside the loop.

retry.hint: How many times did Done! show?

avatar.text: Super! Here's what you learned.

lessons.title: Build a Guessing Game
lessons.goal: to build a real game from print, input, if and a loop.

avatar.text: This is it. Everything you learned, all in one real game. Python picks a secret number, and you have 3 tries to find it!

code_example.description: Watch everything you learned become one game.
code_example.explanation: Line 1 brings in random. Line 2 picks a secret number from 1 to 10, so it is different every game. Line 3 gives you 3 turns.

avatar.text: Inside the loop: ask for a guess, then check it. break stops the loop early when you win. Now let's make it smarter. elif means: else if. It asks a second question.

question.question: Why is the secret number different every game?
options: random picks a new number each time
question.answer: random picks a new number each time
question.explanation: Yes! random.randint(1, 10) picks any number from 1 to 10.

avatar.on_correct: Yes! random.randint(1, 10) picks any number from 1 to 10.
avatar.on_wrong: Not quite. random.randint picks a new number every game.

question.question: break stops the loop early when you win.
question.explanation: Correct! No more guesses needed once you win.

avatar.on_correct: Correct! No more guesses needed once you win.
avatar.on_wrong: Not quite. break jumps out of the loop straight away.

retry.hint: What happens after You win! shows?

question.question: Your turn: give a hint! Add elif so a guess lower than the secret prints Too low!. Play it, then Submit.
question.explanation: Remember: elif goes between the if part and the else part, lined up with them.

code_example.explanation: Remember: elif goes between the if part and the else part, lined up with them.
code_example.starterCode:
import random
secret = random.randint(1, 10)
for turn in range(3):
    guess = int(input("Guess a number from 1 to 10: "))
    if guess == secret:
        print("You win!")
        break
    # TODO: elif guess is less than secret, print  Too low!

    else:
        print("Too high!")
print("The number was", secret)

avatar.before_demo: Before you try, one quick look at the example.
avatar.handoff: Got it? I'll clear the example now.
avatar.on_correct: You did it! You just built a real game with hints.
avatar.on_wrong: Not yet. Write elif guess < secret: lined up with if, then the print on the next line with more spaces.

retry.hint: The < sign means less than. Write elif guess < secret: then print Too low! under it.

points: print and input talk to the player.
if, elif and else make decisions.
A loop gives turns, and random makes every game new.
